messages.Introduction: Attribution assigns the desk's P&L to signals, positions and costs, and the split must add up.
messages.1. What it means to attribute a P&L: An attribution splits realised minus reference P&L into components, plus a residual reported as its own line.
messages.1.1 What daily snapshots miss: Daily snapshots see position P&L; intraday trades and their costs need fill-level records.
messages.1.2 Information and accounting interval: An attribution depends on what was known at each decision and on the accounting interval.
messages.1.3 Two kinds of indicator: Signals drive the desk's trades; state indicators describe market conditions. They call for different methods.
messages.2. The classical answers: Classical splits add up exactly, and each depends on a convention: a benchmark, a factor model, a reference price.
messages.2.1 Allocation, selection, interaction: Brinson splits active return into allocation, selection and interaction, and the three add up to the total.
messages.2.2 A fitted exposure need not be a hold: A regression on index returns gives a fitted exposure, which need not match what the portfolio held.
messages.2.3 Factor return and factor risk: A factor model splits P&L into factor and specific parts; Euler's rule splits risk so that it adds up.
messages.2.4 Estimated components are uncertain: Factor and specific P&L are estimates, with standard errors even when the model is right.
messages.2.5 Spread and inventory: a market maker: A market maker's P&L splits into spread earned and inventory gains; the reference price moves money between them.
messages.3. Attributing a P&L to signals: Signal attribution must model the policy: removing a signal changes the trades, the risk scaling and the costs.
messages.3.1 Stand-alone portfolios as proxies: One run of the policy per signal costs only K runs, but the stand-alone runs need not add up.
messages.3.2 Removing one signal from the full po: Leave-one-out measures what is lost when one signal is removed; these losses need not sum to the P&L.
messages.3.3 Using the optimiser's internal equat: For a known quadratic optimiser, Durin splits the actual position by signal, and the pieces add up exactly.
messages.3.4 Sharing value across coalitions: Shapley shares average each signal's gain over all orders of entry and sum to the gain over the reference policy.
messages.3.5 What the synthetic comparison finds: On a synthetic desk, Shapley stays close to Durin; stand-alone proxies drift as spread and correlation grow.
messages.4. Correlated indicators and the value o: For correlated state indicators, the shares depend on the question asked, which is fixed before the sharing rule.
messages.4.1 Shared information is not a regressi: Regression coefficients swing between near-copies; Shapley shares split what they explain together.
messages.4.2 The game comes before the allocation: R², SHAP and SAGE answer different questions, in different units, and none of them measures realised P&L.
messages.4.3 Importance needs a comparison under: A model fitted to noise still ranks indicators, so the top share is compared with one from a shuffled P&L.
messages.5. Research directions: Project 5.1 fixes which amounts the fill records explain; project 5.2 measures how much each signal earned, both in simulation.
messages.5.1 A reference price for the ledger: Markouts at growing horizons show when the price move after a fill stops reverting; that horizon sets the reference price.
messages.5.2 Signals: how much each one earned: Rerunning the trading policy is expensive; we test when a cheap method gives the same answer, with error bars.
messages.5.3 State indicators and opaque policies: Later work relates spread and inventory P&L to market conditions, and covers policies without usable optimality equations.
